A friend of mine kept telling me I should try spin class with her, and after saying no about ten times over the past few months, I finally gave in.
She promised it would be fun, low pressure, nothing too crazy.
I believed her completely, which, looking back, was my first mistake of the day.
We walked in, and the room was already packed with people who clearly knew what they were doing.
Everyone adjusted their bikes in like two seconds flat, like they'd done it a thousand times before.
I stood there for a solid minute just trying to figure out how the seat even moved up and down.

The instructor turned the lights down low, cranked up the music, and started yelling things like, "Bring it up a level!" I had absolutely no idea what that meant, so I just kind of turned a random dial and hoped for the best, watching everyone else out of the corner of my eye.
For the first five minutes, I actually felt pretty good.
I mean, how hard could pedaling really be?
Then the instructor said we were doing hills, and suddenly my legs felt like they were made of jelly.
Everyone around me kept going like it was absolutely nothing at all.
At one point, I looked down and realized I had somehow turned the resistance all the way up without meaning to.
So while everyone else was casually pedaling along, I was basically trying to move a bike through wet cement.
I couldn't figure out how to turn it back down in time, so I just kept going, sweating way more than anyone else in the entire room.
By the end of the class, I was completely out of breath, and my legs were shaking so badly I almost fell off the bike getting down.
Someone next to me was already packing up her water bottle and towel like she'd just done a light warmup, not an actual workout.
My friend, meanwhile, looked totally fine, barely even breathing hard, and casually asked if I wanted to come back next week.
She even suggested we grab smoothies afterward, like her legs hadn't just done the exact same class mine had.
I just stared at her, trying to figure out if she was secretly part robot.
I told her I needed at least a month to recover, and honestly, I wasn't exaggerating even a little bit.
I couldn't walk up stairs properly for three whole days.
But somehow, a small part of me still wants to go back and prove I can actually do it without turning the bike into a torture device.
We'll see.
